chapter_theme: The Kutralam verses that close the Thiruppadal Thirattu: the beggar's creed in its plainest form (worship, stay where you like, take alms, sleep at the temple gate, go to no one's house even when starving), the heart told again and again not to trust this birth after seeing the corpse hiccup, the pampered body burned on logs, the vultures tear the nine-mouthed bag and the loincloth stripped off kings; the three conches of birth, marriage and death; and three closing claims, that the freed mind stays in silence whatever the body does, that examining pollution itself reveals the one, and that the guru's one word made everything, earth, gods, man and woman, melt.
structure_note: The editorial labels split the chapter by metre: ordinary venbas (412 to 419), venbas with a galloping last line (பின்முடுகு, 420 to 430), a viruttam (431) and two stanzas of another metre (432, 433). The பின்முடுகு venbas 420 to 423 share one form, a question to the heart about rebirth followed by கண்டு, 'having seen', and a scene from the burning ground. 429, 426 and 433 are the chapter's doctrinal verses and stand apart from the exhortations.

412.reading: While the little hall and Siva are close at hand, we went seeking an empty hall; every day the foolish, ignorant heart seeks the place it was born from, and the eye seeks the place it was milked.
412.nuance: சிற்றம்பலம் is the hall of the dance at Chidambaram and, as the Siddhars use it, the small space within where Siva dances; வெற்றம்பலம், the empty hall, is the world outside, or a pun on வெற்று, vain. பிறந்த இடம் and கறந்த இடம் are the womb and the breast, so the heart's lust and the eye's are named by their infant origins.

413.reading: Peacock-woman with the garland of opening buds, those who sought you have now gone; be calm; if you go seeking and think of me, I will kick you in the waist; and if I think of you, kick me.
413.nuance: A verse to a woman, possibly the poet's wife or a courtesan, with the renunciation made mutual and physical: the same kick for either party's lapse. தேறியிரு, be consoled, is the one kind word, and it concerns the other men who have left her.

414.reading: I do not crave alms that will not come past the doorstep, Lord; the whole time I have spent dying of desire is enough, Supreme One; tell me the knowledge that is beyond pointing.
414.nuance: வாசற்படி கடந்து வாராத பிச்சை is read as alms that are not brought out to the door, which the beggar will not go in to fetch (as 416 says outright); it may instead be alms that never leave the giver's house at all. சுட்டிறந்த ஞானம் is taken as knowledge that goes beyond சுட்டு, demonstration or pointing, a term for what cannot be indicated as 'this'; a plain reading, knowledge in which desire is burnt and dead, is also possible, and the pun may be intended.

415.reading: To worship well the one who wears the poisonous serpent, to stay wherever one pleases, to take alms and eat them, and to come and sleep at the holy gate: this alone is happiness.
415.nuance: The whole of the beggar's day in four items, with தானே சுகம், this itself is happiness, as the claim; 417 repeats the formula with praise of Siva as its content. The temple gate (திருவாயில்) is the bed, so the shrine is used as a shelter and not only as a place of worship.

416.reading: If someone seeks out the place where I am and brings food for my hunger with eagerness, I will eat; even if they call me with much insistence I will not go, Hara; even if the body wastes away, from now on I will not go.
416.nuance: A vow stricter than begging: the poet will not enter a house even when invited, and eats only what is carried to him. ஏகம் இளைத்தாலும், even if the body wastes, accepts starvation as the price, which 407 shows being paid.

417.reading: Once you let go, sorrow leaves; the moment the breath leaves, the kin set about burning the body; whatever happens, happens, so at every hour praise and worship Siva alone; I have said it: that itself is happiness.
417.nuance: விட்டுவிடப் போகும் துயர் puts the whole of release in one act of letting go; the kin's haste to burn is the reason. பட்டது படு, let what happens happen, is indifference to outcome rather than fate as a doctrine.

418.reading: Even if breath and body perish, do not earn on this earth the name of sinner; grand display and the garland are not wanted, foolish heart; go about like the dead.
418.nuance: கடம்பு is read as the kadamba garland, standing for finery; it may be a corrupt word. செத்தாரைப் போலே திரி, wander like the dead, is the Siddhars' formula for the jnani alive in the world and is the verse's whole instruction; the garland and display are what the dead do not want.

419.reading: Unknown even to the open void, unseen by orders and by cash in hand, not clinging to those who said 'hold on with love': the sweetness he set in the heart of this sinner, saying 'this'.
419.nuance: The verse is a single inverted sentence whose subject, the sweetness (இனிப்பு) the Lord placed in the heart, comes last. வெட்டவெளி, the open expanse, is the Siddhars' word for the void that is the Lord's place, so a sweetness hidden even from that is beyond the highest state as well as beyond money and command; the phrase பற்றென்றார் பற்றாது is hard and the reading given is a guess. இற்றென, 'as this', may be the guru's pointing or the Lord's.

420.reading: Would anyone trust this birth, my heart, while the hoard lies there and the wife is at the door, having seen, as in a dream, the hiccup, the clenched teeth, the eyes rolled up, the cotton stuffed in, and the bag choke, die and empty itself?
420.nuance: The first of four venbas (420 to 423) on the same frame: a question to the heart about birth, then கண்டு, having seen, and a death scene. Here the scene is the deathbed itself, each symptom a word, with the cotton (பஞ்சு) stuffed in the nostrils of the corpse.

421.reading: You wanted to live still longer, and did not know the nature of the rider of the white bull, my mind; having seen the body that was pampered with cushions for its hands and feet and a mattress, then struck and beaten, laid on logs and burned.
421.nuance: குத்தி மொத்தப்பட்ட, pierced and pounded, may describe the sick body's treatment (massage, surgery) or the corpse being pressed onto the pyre; either way the pampered body ends on the logs. சீலம், the Lord's nature, is what the mind should have known instead of wanting more life.

422.reading: You set your love on the leather bag with nine mouths as if each day were yesterday, my heart, and wandered, having seen the cruel vultures hop and hop, strike off the shirt of skin, bite, tear, peck, cut and eat.
422.nuance: ஒருநாளைப் போலவே, as on one day, is loving the body as if it never changed. The last line is the metre's gallop put to work, seven verbs of the vultures' eating in one breath; சட்டை, the shirt, is the skin they tear off.

423.reading: Do you still consent to be born again, my heart, having seen the double loincloth of those who lived as 'these are kings' stripped off and rolled up and thrown on a log that had already burned?
423.nuance: Even kings go to the fire with one cloth, and that is taken away and thrown on a used log, so the last possession is less than the fuel. இசைவையோ, do you consent, treats rebirth as something the heart agrees to, not something that merely happens.

424.reading: The first conch feeds milk; the middle conch fastens the fine shackle of the thick-haired women; the last conch sounds 'he is gone': is this, or that, the whole of the good we lived on earth?
424.nuance: The conch is the infant's milk feeder, the instrument blown at the wedding and the one blown at the funeral, so one object marks the three events; the shackle (விலங்கு) is marriage. முதல், நடு, கடை சங்கம் also name the three Tamil academies, and the pun makes a life as short as the record of the sangams.

425.reading: The body gathered over so many days, is all of it not food for the earth? Holding the feet of the skilful one, slowly, in the place where night and day are no more, we shall settle in the dwelling above.
425.nuance: மண்டின்பது is read as மண் தின்பது, what the earth eats, so the body collected over a life is returned to the ground that fed it. கங்குல் பகல் அற்ற இடம், where night and day have ceased, is the Siddhars' description of the state beyond the sun and moon of the body, taken plainly as release; மேலைக் குடியிருப்பு is the upper dwelling, heaven or the head.

426.reading: Do not call things 'polluted' and talk of what is fit and unfit; you do not know where the pollution lives; if you examine the pollution itself and stay with it, oneness will show itself, and after that the mind will be free of all disease.
426.nuance: எச்சில் is saliva and the leavings of food, the ordinary thing that pollutes, and the Siddhars' test case for purity rules. The claim is that the rule's own object, examined, dissolves the rule into ஒருமை, oneness; what that oneness is (that all is equally polluted, or that pollution and purity are one) is not said. நிராமயம், without disease, is the Sanskrit term for the healthy or the Absolute, so the mind's cure and its freedom are one word.

427.reading: How many men have dug the pit, how many have touched the breast, how many have pulled at the lip; day after day they speak lies: leave the foolish women of this earth and be saved, be saved, be saved.
427.nuance: The three எத்தனை பேர் make the woman's body a shared thing, and the lies (பொய்) are what each man is told. உய்யடா repeated three times is the chapter's loudest line; the verse addresses men, and its target is the women who take many men, so it is about the courtesan rather than women as such, though it does not draw the line.

428.reading: Reckoning that staying is false and going is true, my heart, do not intend harm to anyone at all; while we hold the fat belly to be ours, the dogs, the jackals, the ghosts and the vultures hold it to be theirs.
428.nuance: The one verse of ethics toward others in the chapter, and it is grounded in impermanence: harming no one follows from the body not being one's own. The scavengers' claim repeats 354, now as a reason for conduct rather than a lament.

429.reading: Whatever work they do, whatever hardship they undergo, the minds of the freed stay in silence; skilfully, like the servant woman who comes playing and swinging both her arms as she walks, her mind is on the water pot on her head.
429.nuance: The figure of the water carrier is exact: the body is free to move and play because the attention is fixed elsewhere, and the pot does not fall. The verse frees the jnani's outer life from any required form, work or austerity, and so stands against the ascetic marks the poet himself lists elsewhere (357, 360); what is required is only where the mind is.

430.reading: In the evening she ground fragrant turmeric and bathed, took trouble and kept vigil, became pregnant, bore him, raised him, gave him a name; if the son she bore turns mad, what can she do after that?
430.nuance: பித்தன், the madman, is the God-mad renunciant the poet calls himself (361, 388), so the verse is his own mother's case stated as anyone's: the whole labour of motherhood undone by the son's renunciation, with no remedy. The turmeric bath and vigil are the woman's observances for conceiving, so the labour begins before the birth as at 391.

431.reading: Splitting your tongue with lies you seek the nine treasures, join women who know no good, split your lips with lies to them and beget children by the swarm, like termites; you do not know how to keep them and cannot abandon them; you have thrust your leg into the split of a wedged tree, like the monkey that shook loose the wedge: you are caught, caught to lie there and writhe.
431.nuance: The monkey that pulled out the wedge from a half-split log and was caught by the testicles is the opening fable of the Panchatantra; here it is the householder's own doing that traps him. புற்றீசல், the winged termites that swarm after rain and die the same night, is the figure for children bred without thought, and the verse's middle line, that one can neither keep them nor leave them, is the trap.

432.reading: The form, the self, youth, the daughter, the mother, the mother-in-law and those who took the ground: in a town, is it justice to celebrate blame? Is the newcomer a pauper, is the potter a dwarf, is the one standing in the middle an idler? The city has been plundered.
432.nuance: The verse is obscure and reads as cipher. நகரம் சூறையானது, the city has been looted, is read by tradition as the body-city plundered by death or by the senses, with the potter (குயவன்) as Brahma who shaped it and the one standing in the middle (நடுநின்றான்) as the soul or the Lord within; on that reading the household figures of line 1 are the body's attachments. A plain reading of a town's quarrel and its sack is possible but gives no connected sense. Every part of the reading given is doubtful.

433.reading: Earth melts, tree melts, maya melts, Vishnu melts, woman melts, man melts, the ways of difference and non-difference melt, the Lord melts, the Mother seated where he melts melts, the one on the serpent bed melts: so is the one word the guru, who thinks and melts, spoke to me.
433.nuance: உருகும், melts, eleven times, is the word for the devotee's melting in love, here applied to everything down to maya and to the Lord himself. பேதாபேத வகை, the kinds of bheda and abheda, names the Vedantic positions and melts them too; whether the one word (ஓர் மொழி) is a mantra, a teaching, or the word 'melt' is not said. The work ends on the guru's word, as 378 did.

links.note: Tirumular makes Siva himself the renouncer who dwells in the burning ground and eats alms; Pattinathar's happiness is to worship the serpent-wearer, take alms and eat, and sleep at the temple gate. The beggar's life is the Lord's own in one and the devotee's in the other, and both call it the renouncer's.

Pattinathar names taking alms and eating them among the four things that alone are happiness; the Kural says that if one must live by begging, let the world's maker wander and perish. On the Kural's plain reading begging is a life not worth the world's making; for Pattinathar it is the whole of the good life. As at 357, the conflict holds unless the Kural is confined to the needy.

The Kural says not asking, even from those who give gladly, is worth ten million times more; Pattinathar goes beyond not asking: he will not go even when called with insistence, and eats only what is brought to where he sits, though the body waste. The Kural's restraint on asking becomes a refusal of the giver's house.

The Naladiyar's worthy man goes before no one except those who embrace him and say 'come in, eat'; Pattinathar will not go even to those, and accepts food only if it is carried to him with eagerness. The Naladiyar allows the welcoming host as the one exception; Pattinathar removes it.

Tirumular's Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while their senses and body remain intact, set against ritual purifiers and chattering knowers; Pattinathar tells his heart to want no display or garland and to go about like the dead. The same formula for the jnani's outer life, in Tirumular as description and in Pattinathar as instruction to himself.

The vultures at the stinking body: the Naladiyar asks whether those who praise sandal and garlands have not seen vultures crowd in and tear at the stinking cart once its axle breaks; Pattinathar's heart is asked whether it has not seen the vultures hop, strip the skin and eat. Both end the body's story at the birds and use the sight as the argument against loving it.

Sivavakkiyar turns the rule of leavings on the one who keeps it, since the hand and the water are already touched by mouths; Pattinathar goes a step further and makes the saliva itself the object of inquiry, so that examining it reveals oneness and heals the mind. Sivavakkiyar refutes the rule, Pattinathar makes its object a means.

Tirumular says there is no need of purification for one who stands free of pollution; Pattinathar says one who examines the pollution itself and stays with it comes to oneness and a mind without disease. In both the purity rite is superseded by a state, though Tirumular's state is being clean of pollution and Pattinathar's is seeing through it.

The Kural asks why one who knows what is hurtful to his own life does hurtful things to other beings; Pattinathar tells the heart not to intend harm to anyone, since the body one would protect by harming belongs already to the dogs and vultures. Both ground harmlessness in the self, the Kural in the self's own knowledge of hurt, Pattinathar in the self's having no body to defend.

Tirumular says silence is when speech and mind are both still, and one whose speech alone is silent is merely mute; Pattinathar's freed ones keep the mind in silence while the body works, suffers or plays like the water carrier swinging her arms. Both place silence in the mind and not in the mouth or the limbs; Pattinathar adds that the limbs may do anything.

357 makes the renunciant's marks (loincloth, bowl, verandah, poor food) the wealth without lack, and 360 and 363 repeat the inventory; 429 says the freed mind stays in silence whatever the work or austerity, so that no outward form is the mark. The later verse does not cancel the beggar's way but denies that it is required.

source_issues: The metre labels (பொதுவெண்பா, பின்முடுகு வெண்பா, விருத்தம், இதுவுமதுவேறு) are a modern editor's headings.
417 has the venba's third line run into the second after the dash (பட்டதுபட் டெந்நேரமுஞ்சிவனையேத்துங்கள்போற்றுங்கள்), so the line break is lost.
418 line 3 கடம்பும் is doubtful in sense; read as the kadamba garland.
431 line 1 is spaced (நாப்பிளக்கப் பொய்யுரைத்து) unlike the rest of the work; 432 and 433 return to unspaced text.
432 is obscure throughout and may be corrupt; the reading given is a guess at a body-city cipher.
